01

### A requirement comes in

A company tells us the role, the stack, the level and the timeline. If a matching cohort is already running, we point at it. If not, we design one around the requirement.

heading: Mission / why it exists
text:
## Mission / why it exists
ABTalks turns visible, dated work into proof that recruiters can inspect in a browser. The premise is that consistent, publicly-dated work is a stronger, more inspectable signal of skill than a private credential or resume line alone.

heading: Philosophy / build-in-public model
text:
## Philosophy / build-in-public model
The core operating loop is: learn daily, build and showcase, then get hired. Participants work in the open rather than complete private coursework — pushing code to GitHub and posting progress on LinkedIn as they go. Visibility and consistency (streaks, public repos, dated posts) are treated as central to the model, not an optional add-on.

heading: Proof-of-work concept
text:
## Proof-of-work concept
"Proof of work" on ABTalks means a public, dated, externally-verifiable trail of what a participant built and learned:
- A GitHub repository (for the Claude Challenge, a dedicated repo organized `Day1/` … `Day60/`) showing real commits over time
- LinkedIn posts describing what was built, key learnings, and a demo/screenshot
- Tracked streaks and completion counts that make consistency visible
- Certificates (some with QR-based verification) as a portable credential of completion

This proof-of-work trail — not a private grade or credential — is what's meant to make a participant discoverable to recruiters.

heading: Synergy Points (SP)
text:
## Synergy Points (SP)
Synergy Points (often abbreviated as **SP**) are the community reward system on ABTalks. They are designed to recognize and reward consistency and community growth.
- **How they are earned:** Participants earn SP primarily by submitting their daily challenge tasks (earning up to 15 SP per day: 5 base points + 5 for attaching a GitHub repo + 5 for attaching a LinkedIn post) and by referring friends to join the platform (earning 3 SP per successful signup).
- **How they are used:** Accumulated Synergy Points can be redeemed in the **Marketplace** (`/marketplace`) for various rewards, goodies, or special opportunities.
- **Important note:** SP is not a currency, has no cash value, and cannot be exchanged for money.

heading: Platform Mechanics
text:
## Platform Mechanics
ABTalks has several core platform mechanics that apply across the challenges:
- **Leaderboard**: The global leaderboard is ranked primarily by **Days Completed** (highest to lowest), followed by **Current Streak** (highest to lowest), then **Longest Streak** (highest to lowest), and finally by **Start Date** (earliest to latest).
- **Quizzes**: Only the current week's quiz is available to participants, based on their total days completed.
- **Referrals**: Every participant has a unique 6-character referral code. When someone signs up using this code, the referrer instantly earns 3 Synergy Points (SP).

heading: AI Cohort
text:
## AI Cohort
The AI Cohort is a 31-day program for building and deploying a production-grade enterprise AI chatbot.

Core facts:
- 31 days end to end
- 8 gated phases
- Roughly 2–4 hours per day
- Free for participants
- Uses free tools such as Ollama, Groq, and Chroma

Coverage includes RAG, embeddings, agents, MCP, guardrails, Docker, Kubernetes, evaluation, and deployment.

heading: 8-phase / 31-day breakdown

| Phase | Days | Title | Focus |

| 1 | 1–3 | Env & Tooling | Local AI stack, Git, Ollama |
| 2 | 4–6 | Data | Coverage data & structured queries |
| 3 | 7–10 | Embeddings & Vector | Knowledge base + retrieval |
| 4 | 11–15 | LLM & Prompting | Prompting, fine-tune basics |
| 5 | 16–20 | App Build | Streamlit chatbot + FastAPI |
| 6 | 21–24 | Agentic + MCP | Tools, agents, MCP servers |

heading: Cohort flow
text:
## Cohort flow
1. Apply — confirm laptop and GitHub setup.
2. 31 days of missions — build locally; GitHub artifacts verified.
3. AI interview — Upon completion, participants unlock a 15-minute real-time voice interview evaluated by AI.
4. Recruiter visibility — Recruiters use the Talent Portal (`/talent`) to view ranked participant profiles, which include their mission portfolios and interview summaries. Note: Participant phone numbers and entry details are never exposed to recruiters.

## Eligibility — who can join ABTalks programs
ABTalks programs are open to college students at any year of study — first
year through final year — across any branch or degree (BTech, BE, or
otherwise), as well as recent graduates and working professionals. There is
no minimum year-of-study requirement for the 60-Day Coding Challenge, the
60-Day Claude AI Challenge, or the AI Cohort. A first-year, second-year,
third-year, or final-year BTech student can all participate; so can someone
who has already graduated or is currently employed.

Program-specific eligibility notes:
- 60-Day Coding Challenge, 60-Day Claude AI Challenge: open to any year of
  study, any branch, no prerequisites required to start.
- AI Cohort: open to students and recent grads who meet the stated
  prerequisites (Python fundamentals, SQL, Git/GitHub, REST APIs, JavaScript
  & React basics) — see `ai-cohort.md`. Year of study isn't itself a
  restriction; the prerequisites are what determine readiness.
- Vibe Code Hackathon (ViCodathon): eligibility is Indian college students;
  see `vicodathon.md` for team-size and submission requirements.

Source: `abtalks.md` ("Audience"), `claude-challenge.md`, and
`testimonials.md` (the Claude Challenge testimonial roster includes a 20+
year IT leader, confirming the program isn't restricted by career stage
either).

heading: For students
text:
## For students
**Q: What's the difference between the 60-Day Coding Challenge and the
60-Day Claude AI Challenge?**
A: The 60-Day Coding Challenge lets you pick a broad domain (Software
Engineering / Data Science / AI) and build daily projects in it. The 60-Day
Claude AI Challenge is specifically about mastering Claude and prompt
engineering, with a 10-day capstone to ship a deployed product. Both are
free.

**Q: Which program should I pick if I want a job?**
A: If you already meet the prerequisites (Python, SQL, Git, React basics),
the 31-Day AI Cohort is the most jobs-oriented — it ends in a real-time AI
voice interview and recruiter visibility. If you're earlier in your journey,
do the 60-Day Coding Challenge in your target track to build a portfolio
first.

**Q: Do I need a laptop with a GPU?**
A: No. The AI Cohort explicitly asks for ≥8 GB RAM only, and uses
Ollama / Groq / Chroma — all free-tier / local. No paid API keys required.

**Q: Do I need to know how to code?**
A: For the 60-Day Coding Challenge and AI Cohort, yes — pick the track that
matches your current level. For the 60-Day Claude AI Challenge, you can
start as a beginner; the daily tasks are prompts you run, not code you write
from scratch (though the outputs are apps you'll deploy).

**Q: What if I miss a day?**
A: You can keep going, but the missed day breaks your streak. Submissions
follow IST day boundaries.

**Q: How much time per day does it take?**
A: 31-Day AI Cohort: roughly 2–4 hours/day. 60-Day Claude Challenge: varies
by task, generally 30–90 minutes. 60-Day Coding Challenge: designed as "one
task a day."

**Q: What are the community rules?**
A: Foul language, harassment, or harmful messaging results in a permanent
ban. Plagiarism or platform misuse results in a 60-day challenge ban. See
`community.md`.

**Q: How do I join the community?**
A: Use the "Join now" link on the official website for the WhatsApp
community (invite links rotate, so there's no fixed URL to give out here).
Also Discord, LinkedIn, Instagram, YouTube, X — all under `abtalksonai`. See
`socials-and-contact.md`.

**Q: How do I apply for placements or internships through ABTalks?**
A: Email your resume, cover letter, and anything else relevant (portfolio
link, GitHub, LinkedIn, project links) to team@abtalks.in. The team reviews
applications and routes strong profiles to the hiring partner network.
Openings themselves are also shared inside the ABTalks WhatsApp community,
so it's worth joining if you haven't already.

**Q: Do I need to have finished a program before applying?**
A: No — you can email team@abtalks.in anytime. But a completed program gives
you public artifacts to point to, which is exactly the signal recruiters in
the network look for.

**Q: What should go in the application email?**
A: Resume, cover letter, and links that prove work — GitHub, deployed
projects, LinkedIn build log, ABTalks profile, portfolio site — plus
anything else material to the role you're targeting.

permanently ban plagiarism across all programs.

heading: Official challenge guidelines
text:
## Official challenge guidelines
Source: `public/documents/ABTalks-60-Day-Challenge-Guidelines.pdf` (present in this repository and linked from the live site — authoritative for this program).

### GitHub repository setup

- Create ONE dedicated GitHub repository — it is the official record of the 60 days
- Organize it day by day: `Day1/`, `Day2/`, `Day3/`, `Day4/` ... through `Day60/`
- Each day's folder holds that day's prompts, outputs, code, notes, and screenshots
- A clean, well-structured repo makes progress easy to review

### Sharing progress on LinkedIn

Each post should clearly cover:
- What was completed and what was built or explored
- Key learnings, insights, and any real-world applications
- Screenshots or a short demo of the result

Every post must tag all three accounts: `@AnilBajpai`, `@ABTalksOnAI`, and `@Anthropic`, so the team can track participation and amplify the work.

### What counts as a submission

A day is complete only when all three steps are done:
1. Work is pushed to the GitHub repository
2. Progress is shared in a LinkedIn post
3. All required tags are included in that post

Missing any one of the three steps means that day's submission may not count.

### Consistency and streaks

- Progress is tracked on a 60-day streak heatmap
- A participant's current streak is based on making an on-time submission every day
- Submissions made late do not count towards the current streak
- Missing a day does not remove a participant from the challenge — the streak resets to 0, but participation continues; the goal is to keep going
- Consistency is weighed when the team considers: goodies, community recognition, and special opportunities

### Certificates

- A verified Certificate of Completion is issued when a participant completes the final **Day 60** submission AND has completed **at least 50 days** in total throughout the challenge.
- Certificates include a unique ID (`ABT-XX-XXXXX`) and a QR code for public verification.
- Missing a day does not remove a participant from the challenge — the streak resets, but participation continues; the goal is to keep going
- Consistency is weighed when the team considers: certificates, goodies, community recognition, and special opportunities

### What makes a strong participant

Participants who make the strongest impact consistently bring:
- Daily participation — an uninterrupted, visible streak
- A clean repository — clear folders, easy to navigate
- Professional documentation — well-written, high-quality posts
- Thoughtful reflection — real learnings, not just outputs

The goal isn't 60 tasks — it's a public record of real growth.

heading: Day 1 (Module 1): VS Code & Python Environment Setup
text:
Module 1: Environment & Tooling

Brief:
## Mission: VS Code & Python Environment Setup

Install VS Code and Python, and get comfortable running Python code inside VS Code - the foundation for every day that follows. **Stack for this program:** VS Code + Ollama + Python + React.

**Concepts to learn**

- Why VS Code is the standard free editor for this program, and what the extension ecosystem gives you
- Installing Python and verifying the install from a terminal
- The VS Code Python extension (Microsoft) + Pylance for IntelliSense, plus the optional Jupyter extension
- Running a Python file from inside VS Code
- Virtual environments (`.venv`) and why every project gets its own
- Selecting the right Python interpreter for a project in VS Code

### Build steps

1. **Install VS Code:**
   - Go to https://code.visualstudio.com and click Download for Mac (or Windows)
   - **macOS:** open the downloaded .zip and drag Visual Studio Code into your Applications folder
   - **Windows:** run the installer, keeping default options ("Add to PATH" checked)
   - Launch VS Code

2. *(macOS, recommended)* **Enable the `code` terminal command:**
   - Press `Cmd+Shift+P`
   - Type "Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH" → Enter
   - This lets you type `code .` from any terminal to open that folder in VS Code

3. **Install Python:**
   - Go to https://www.python.org/downloads/ and download the latest Python 3.x
   - **macOS:** run the .pkg installer
   - **Windows:** run the installer and check **"Add python.exe to PATH"** before clicking Install

4. **Verify the install:**
   - Open a terminal in VS Code (Ctrl+` / View → Terminal)
   - Run `python3 --version` (macOS) or `python --version` (Windows)
   - You should see something like Python 3.12.x

5. **Install the Python extension:**
   - Open the Extensions panel (`Cmd+Shift+X` / `Ctrl+Shift+X`)
   - Search "Python" and install the one published by **Microsoft** (includes Pylance)
   - Optionally also install "Jupyter" (Microsoft)

6. **Create a project folder and hello file:**
   - File → Open Folder (create/open a projects folder)
   - Create a file named `hello.py` containing `print("Hello from Python!")`

7. **Run it:**
   - Click the Play button in the top right, **or**
   - Right-click in the editor → "Run Python File in Terminal"
   - Output appears in the integrated terminal at the bottom
   - If prompted to select an interpreter: `Cmd+Shift+P` → "Python: Select Interpreter" → pick your installed Python 3.x

8. **Set up a virtual environment** (recommended per project):
   - In the terminal run `python3 -m venv .venv`
   - Activate it:
     - **macOS/Linux:** `source .venv/bin/activate`
     - **Windows:** `.venv\Scripts\activate`
   - Your terminal prompt should now show `(.venv)` at the start

9. **Confirm the venv works:**
   - Run `pip install requests`
   - When VS Code asks to select the `.venv` interpreter, click **Yes**
   - Or: `Cmd+Shift+P` → "Python: Select Interpreter" → choose the one showing `.venv`


### Submit your answers

Answer these below in order (they prove you actually did the setup):

1. What is the name of the **folder** created by the `python3 -m venv .venv` command?
2. Which **company/publisher** publishes the official Python extension for VS Code?
3. Which **test package** did you install to confirm your virtual environment works?


Objectives:
- Install VS Code and the Microsoft Python extension (+ Pylance)
- Install and verify Python from the terminal
- Run a Python file inside VS Code
- Create a per-project .venv and select it as the interpreter

Tools:
- VS Code
- Python 3
- pip

Videos:
- How to Setup Python in Visual Studio Code (2026)
- Setting up VS Code for Python Beginners — official
- Setup Python in VS Code on Windows 10/11

heading: Day 2 (Module 1): Ollama (Local LLM) + AI Coding Assistant Setup
text:
Module 1: Environment & Tooling

Brief:
## Mission: Your own local AI, running on your laptop

Today you install **Ollama** and run an open coding model **fully locally** - free, no API key, works offline. Then you wire it into VS Code as your AI pair programmer. This local model also powers your chatbot's LLM calls later in the program, so nothing in these 31 days requires a paid subscription.

### Build steps

1. **Install Ollama:**
   - Go to https://ollama.com and click Download for macOS/Windows/Linux
   - **macOS:** open the .zip/.dmg, move Ollama to Applications, and launch it (menu-bar icon appears)
   - **Windows:** run the installer; Ollama runs in the system tray

2. **Verify in a terminal:**
   - Run `ollama --version`

3. **Pull a coding model sized to your machine's RAM:**
   - **8 GB:** `ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:3b`
   - **16 GB** (best all-round default for this course): `ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:7b`
   - **32 GB+:** `ollama pull qwen2.5-coder:14b` (or deepseek-coder-v2)
   - The first pull downloads several GB - let it finish

4. **Test the model directly:**
   - Run `ollama run qwen2.5-coder:7b` (swap in whichever size you pulled)
   - Type a question, e.g. "write a python function to reverse a string"
   - Confirm you get a sensible answer, then type `/bye` to exit
   - Ollama now serves an API at `http://localhost:11434` whenever it's running (no separate "start server" step)

5. **Option A - GitHub Copilot Free + Ollama** (recommended if you have a GitHub account):
   - Open Extensions (`Cmd+Shift+X` / `Ctrl+Shift+X`)
   - Search "GitHub Copilot" and Install
   - This usually installs GitHub Copilot Chat too - install it separately if not
   - Reload VS Code if prompted

6. **Sign in to Copilot:**
   - Click the Copilot icon in the bottom-right status bar
   - Choose "Sign in to use Copilot"
   - Log in to GitHub in the browser and click Authorize
   - Back in VS Code, the status bar icon should no longer show an error badge

7. **Open the Chat panel:**
   - `Cmd+Ctrl+I` (macOS) / `Ctrl+Alt+I` (Windows), **or**
   - Click the chat bubble icon in the title bar / Activity Bar
   - The chat panel opens (usually on the right), labeled "Chat"

8. **Open the model picker:**
   - At the bottom of the chat input box, click the model dropdown (e.g. "GPT-4.1" or "Auto")
   - Click "Manage Models..." at the bottom of the list
   - (In some versions: gear icon → "Manage Language Models")

9. **Add Ollama as a provider:**
   - In the provider list, select **Ollama**
   - Ensure the Ollama app is running (menu-bar/tray icon) - VS Code queries `http://localhost:11434`
   - Check the box next to your model (e.g. `qwen2.5-coder:7b`) and press OK
   - If nothing is listed:
     - Run `ollama list` to confirm models exist
     - Run `curl http://localhost:11434` to confirm the server responds ("Ollama is running")

10. **Select and use your local model:**
    - Click the model dropdown again - your model appears under an "Ollama" section
    - Select it and prompt e.g. "write a python function that checks if a number is prime"
    - Confirm the response is generated 100% locally (works offline)
    - Switch between local and Copilot cloud models any time from the same dropdown

11. **Option B - no GitHub account?** Use Cline instead:
    - Extensions view → search "Cline" (publisher saoudrizwan) → Install
    - Open its settings gear → set API Provider to **Ollama**
    - Base URL: `http://localhost:11434`
    - Pick your pulled model - no sign-in required
    - Everywhere this course says "ask Copilot" / "open Chat," use Cline's panel instead


### Submit your answers

1. On which **localhost port** does Ollama serve its API?
2. Which terminal command **lists the models** you have pulled?
3. What do you type inside an `ollama run` chat session to **exit**?


Objectives:
- Run an open LLM fully locally with Ollama
- Pick a model size that fits your RAM
- Wire the local model into VS Code (Copilot Free or Cline)

Tools:
- Ollama
- qwen2.5-coder
- GitHub Copilot Free / Cline

Videos:
- How to Install Ollama and Run Models Locally
- Ollama Beginner Setup: Install, Run Models, Test the API
- GitHub Copilot with Ollama: Local AI Models in VS Code

heading: Day 3 (Module 1): First Python Project, a Local Chatbot & Git/GitHub
text:
Module 1: Environment & Tooling

Brief:
## Mission: First AI project - local chatbot, FastAPI skeleton & Node

Hands-on build (~3.5–4 hrs): create your first AI-assisted Python app, a command-line chatbot against your local Ollama model, scaffold the FastAPI backend this course extends, and install Node.js. When you finish the build steps, ship the artifacts to **your program repo** (the GitHub repository you registered when you applied) so we can verify them.

### Your repo layout (verification checks these exact paths)

After local work in `~/projects/my-first-app`, copy these into your program repo:

```
your-program-repo/
├── main.py                         ← AI-assisted first script
├── chatbot.py                      ← local Ollama CLI chatbot
├── coverage-chatbot-api/
│   ├── main.py                     ← FastAPI /health (grows later)
│   ├── requirements.txt
│   └── README.md                   ← optional inside the API folder
├── .gitignore
└── README.md
```

### Build steps

1. **Create a new project:**
   - Run `mkdir ~/projects/my-first-app && cd ~/projects/my-first-app`
   - Run `code .` to open it in VS Code

2. **Create a virtual environment for this project:**
   - Open VS Code's terminal (Ctrl+` / View → Terminal)
   - Run `python3 -m venv .venv`
   - Activate it:
     - **macOS:** `source .venv/bin/activate`
     - **Windows:** `.venv\Scripts\activate`
   - When VS Code asks "select this environment?", click **Yes**
   - Or: `Cmd+Shift+P` → "Python: Select Interpreter" → `.venv`

3. **Create `main.py` and write code with AI help:**
   - As you type, Copilot suggests completions in gray - press **Tab** to accept
   - For a bigger ask: put your cursor in the file, press `Cmd+I` / `Ctrl+I` (inline chat)
   - Prompt e.g. "write a function that fetches a URL and returns the JSON" - code is inserted in place
   - Use the full chat panel for bigger questions, then click **Apply/Insert** on code blocks

4. **Try the other AI shortcuts:**
   - Highlight any code → right-click → **Copilot**
   - Try **Explain / Fix / Generate Tests**
   - Read what each one produces

5. **Run and debug it:**
   - Click the **▶ button** (top right) **or** run `python main.py` in the terminal
   - To debug: click just left of a line number to set a breakpoint
   - Press **F5** and choose "Python File"
   - Step through and inspect variables

6. **Install the Ollama Python client** in this project's venv:
   - Run `pip install ollama`

7. **Build a mini project** - a command-line chatbot against your local model. Create `chatbot.py`:

```python
import ollama

history = []
print("Local chatbot - type 'quit' to exit")
while True:
    user = input("\nYou: ")
    if user.lower() == "quit":
        break
    history.append({"role": "user", "content": user})
    reply = ollama.chat(model="qwen2.5-coder:7b", messages=history)
    text = reply["message"]["content"]
    history.append({"role": "assistant", "content": text})
    print(f"\nAI: {text}")
```

8. **Run the chatbot and verify memory:**
   - Run `python chatbot.py`
   - Have a short back-and-forth
   - Ask a follow-up that only makes sense if it remembers the earlier message
   - Confirm the model uses conversation history

9. **Scaffold the FastAPI backend skeleton:**
   - Create a new folder (e.g. `coverage-chatbot-api`)
   - Ask Copilot's chat panel to: "scaffold a FastAPI app with a /health endpoint returning {status: ok}, plus requirements.txt and a README"
   - Review what it generates before accepting

10. **Install and run the FastAPI app:**
    - Run `pip install -r requirements.txt`
    - Run `uvicorn main:app --reload`
    - Confirm `/health` responds at `localhost:8000/health` in your browser
    - Later days (chat API, Docker, Kubernetes) extend this same backend

11. **Install Node.js:**
    - Check first: `node -v` in the VS Code terminal
    - If missing: download the LTS version from https://nodejs.org, install it, then restart VS Code


### Ship to your program repo

Copy `main.py`, `chatbot.py`, and the `coverage-chatbot-api/` folder into **your program repo** root. Add a root `.gitignore` containing at least: `.venv/`, `__pycache__/`, `*.pyc`, `.env`. Update the root `README.md` (what this project is - healthcare coverage chatbot, 31-day build - your name, and today's progress). Then commit and push: `git add . && git commit -m "day 3: first app + chatbot + FastAPI skeleton" && git push`. Hit **Verify my repo** below - the checks fetch your pushed files.

### Submit your answers

Answer these below in order (they prove you actually did the build):

1. In the Day 3 `chatbot.py` sample, which **model name** is passed to `ollama.chat`?
2. What is the **folder name** for the FastAPI scaffold (the backend skeleton)?
3. Which terminal command checks whether **Node.js** is installed?


Objectives:
- Build an AI-assisted first Python app in VS Code
- Call a local Ollama model from Python with conversation history
- Scaffold a FastAPI /health skeleton in coverage-chatbot-api
- Install Node.js LTS for later tooling

Tools:
- Python
- ollama (pip)
- FastAPI
- uvicorn
- GitHub Copilot / Cline
- Node.js

Videos:
- Using Git with Visual Studio Code — official tutorial
- Ollama-Powered AI Chatbot with Python

heading: Day 4 (Module 2): Reading & Processing Structured Data
text:
Module 2: Data Foundations

Brief:
## Mission: Ingest and query the coverage data your chatbot will answer from

Today you build the structured data layer behind the healthcare coverage chatbot. You'll create **synthetic** (fake) plans and claims datasets, clean them with pandas, load them into a local SQLite database, and write SQL queries that answer realistic member questions. Use synthetic data only - never real member PHI. Expect about **2–3 hours**.

**Concepts to learn**

- **Loading data with pandas** - CSV/Excel/JSON into DataFrames; filtering, joins, and cleaning
- **SQL fundamentals** - SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY, and nested queries
- **Connecting Python to a database** - SQLite for local development (today); Postgres via SQLAlchemy is the production pattern you'll see later - you do **not** need SQLAlchemy for this mission
- **Basic data cleaning** - nulls, type coercion, and deduplication

### Your repo layout (verification checks these exact paths)

```
your-program-repo/
├── data/
│   ├── plans.csv
│   └── claims.csv
├── coverage.db
├── structured_queries.md
├── notebooks/
│   └── day04-ingestion-lab.ipynb   ← optional workspace
├── chatbot.py                      ← from Day 3
└── backend/                        ← from Day 3
```

### Build steps

1. **Install dependencies** in your activated venv:
   - Run `pip install pandas openpyxl`

2. **Create synthetic sample datasets** (fake data only):
   - Make a `data/` folder
   - Save these two CSVs exactly:

   **`data/plans.csv`**

```csv
plan_id,plan_name,monthly_premium,annual_deductible,copay_pct,coverage_type,network_tier
P101,Gold PPO,500,2000,10,PPO,Gold
P102,Silver HMO,300,1500,20,HMO,Silver
P103,Bronze HMO,150,1000,30,HMO,Bronze
```

   **`data/claims.csv`**

```csv
claim_id,member_id,plan_id,procedure,claim_amount,status,date_filed
C1001,M1001,P101,X-ray,250,Pending,2023-04-01
C1002,M1001,P101,Surgery,1200,Approved,2023-03-15
C1003,M1002,P102,X-ray,150,Denied,2023-04-05
C1004,M1002,P102,Surgery,900,Approved,2023-03-20
C1005,M1003,P103,X-ray,50,Pending,2023-04-10
```

3. **Load and clean the CSVs:**
   - Load both with `pd.read_csv()`
   - Inspect with `.info()` and `.head()`
   - Drop duplicates
   - Fill or drop nulls
   - Coerce `date_filed` to datetime

4. **Create the SQLite database:**
   - Create `coverage.db` with Python's `sqlite3` module
   - Load the cleaned DataFrames via `df.to_sql()` (tables for plans and claims)

5. **Write and test 5 SQL queries** mapped to realistic member questions:
   - "What's the deductible on the Gold PPO plan?"
   - "How many claims are pending for member M1001?"
   - "Which plans have a monthly premium under $400?"
   - A JOIN between claims and plans
   - A top-N query (e.g. most claimed procedures)

6. **Save your work for later:**
   - Save each query and its output in `structured_queries.md`

7. **Ship to your program repo:**
   - Commit and push
   - Hit **Verify my repo** below - the checks fetch your pushed files
   - Tip: `notebooks/day04-ingestion-lab.ipynb` is a convenient workspace for the lab
   - Deliverables at the paths above are what get verified



Objectives:
- Load and clean structured coverage CSVs with pandas (DataFrames, nulls, types, dedupe)
- Write SQL with SELECT, WHERE, JOIN, GROUP BY against plans and claims
- Connect Python to SQLite and load cleaned tables into coverage.db
- Document five working queries mapped to sample member questions in structured_queries.md

Tools:
- pandas
- SQLite
- SQL

Videos:
- Pandas & Python for Data Analysis — freeCodeCamp
- SQL Tutorial — Full Database Course for Beginners

heading: Day 5 (Module 2): Reading & Processing Unstructured Data
text:
Module 2: Data Foundations

Brief:
## Mission: Extract usable text from the documents your chatbot will answer from

Today you build the unstructured-data layer behind the healthcare coverage chatbot. You'll pull text from policy PDFs, claim-form Word docs, scanned enrollment forms (OCR), and a public provider/FAQ page - then clean and save the results. Use **synthetic or publicly published templates only** - never real member PHI. Expect about **3 hours**.

**Concepts to learn**

- **Text extraction from PDFs/Docs** - `pdfplumber`, `PyPDF2`, `python-docx`
- **OCR for scanned documents** - Tesseract / `pytesseract` + `pdf2image`
- **Web scraping basics** for pulling public documentation - `BeautifulSoup`, `requests`
- **Normalizing extracted text** - removing headers/footers, fixing encoding issues, de-duplication

### Your repo layout (verification checks these exact paths)

```
your-program-repo/
├── raw_text/
│   ├── benefits.txt              ← from Summary of Benefits PDF
│   ├── claims_process.txt        ← from claims-process Word doc
│   └── enrollment.txt            ← from scanned enrollment form (OCR)
├── data/                         ← from Day 4
├── coverage.db                   ← from Day 4
├── chatbot.py                    ← from Day 3
└── backend/                      ← from Day 3
```

### Build steps

1. **Install extraction tools:**
   - In your activated venv, run:
     `pip install pdfplumber pypdf python-docx pytesseract pdf2image beautifulsoup4 requests`
   - Install the Tesseract OCR binary for your OS

2. **Gather 3 sample documents** (synthetic or publicly published templates only):
   - A "Summary of Benefits and Coverage"-style PDF
   - A claims-process Word doc
   - A scanned enrollment form image/PDF

3. **Extract text from PDF and Word:**
   - Benefits PDF → `pdfplumber` (`page.extract_text()` per page)
   - Claims-process doc → `python-docx` (`paragraph.text`)

4. **OCR the scanned enrollment form:**
   - Convert pages with `pdf2image.convert_from_path()`
   - Run `pytesseract.image_to_string()` on each page image
   - Note any OCR accuracy issues with handwriting or checkboxes

5. **Scrape one public webpage:**
   - e.g. a sample provider-network or FAQ page
   - Use `requests` + `BeautifulSoup`
   - Extract only the main article/body text (strip nav/footer/ads)

6. **Clean and save extracted text:**
   - Strip extra whitespace and fix encoding
   - Save each document source as a separate `.txt` in `raw_text/`
   - At minimum: `benefits.txt`, `claims_process.txt`, and `enrollment.txt`

7. **Ship to your program repo:**
   - Commit and push
   - Hit **Verify my repo** below - the checks fetch your pushed files

**Deliverable:** 3 cleaned text files extracted from a benefits PDF, a claims-process doc, and a scanned enrollment form (`raw_text/benefits.txt`, `raw_text/claims_process.txt`, `raw_text/enrollment.txt`).



Objectives:
- Extract text from PDFs and Word docs with pdfplumber and python-docx
- Run OCR on scanned enrollment forms with pytesseract + pdf2image
- Scrape a public provider/FAQ page with BeautifulSoup and requests
- Normalize extracted text and save cleaned .txt files under raw_text/

Tools:
- pdfplumber
- python-docx
- pytesseract
- BeautifulSoup

Videos:
- Web Scraping with Python — Beautiful Soup Crash Course
- Extract Text from Scanned PDFs using OCR (Tesseract)

heading: Day 6 (Module 2): Building the Knowledge Base
text:
Module 2: Data Foundations

Brief:
## Mission: Building the Knowledge Base

Turn cleaned plan/claims data and policy documents into a unified, chunked knowledge base ready for embedding. Expect about **2–3 hours**.

**Concepts to learn**

- **Document chunking strategies** - fixed-size, recursive character splitting, semantic chunking
- **Chunk size and overlap trade-offs** - how they affect retrieval quality
- **Metadata design** - `source`, `section`, `plan_type`, document type (critical for filtering later)
- **Knowledge base schema** - a JSON/JSONL shape that both SQL plan rows and policy-document chunks can populate

### Your repo layout (verification checks these exact paths)

```
your-program-repo/
├── knowledge_base.jsonl          ← today's deliverable (one JSON object per line)
├── raw_text/                     ← from Day 5
│   ├── benefits.txt
│   ├── claims_process.txt
│   └── enrollment.txt
├── data/                         ← from Day 4
│   ├── plans.csv
│   └── claims.csv
├── coverage.db                   ← from Day 4
├── chatbot.py
└── coverage-chatbot-api/
```

### Build steps

1. **Install a text splitter** in your activated venv:
   - Run `pip install langchain-text-splitters`
   - Or write a small recursive splitter yourself if you prefer

2. **Load your Day 5 + Day 4 inputs:**
   - Read all `.txt` files from `raw_text/` (`benefits.txt`, `claims_process.txt`, `enrollment.txt`)
   - Export Day 4 plans (from `data/plans.csv` or `coverage.db`) into one chunk per plan, e.g. `"Gold PPO: $350/month premium, $1,500 deductible, 20% coinsurance, network: national"`

3. **Chunk the policy / benefits text** with:
   - `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter(chunk_size=500, chunk_overlap=50)`
   - Prefer keeping coverage-relevant sections as distinct chunks where possible:
     - exclusions
     - covered services
     - claims process

4. **Attach metadata to every chunk** - each record must include:

```json
{
  "id": "...",
  "text": "...",
  "source_file": "...",
  "source_type": "structured|unstructured",
  "plan_type": "...",
  "section": "coverage|exclusions|claims|enrollment",
  "ingested_at": "..."
}
```

   - Plan rows → `source_type: structured`
   - Policy `.txt` chunks → `source_type: unstructured`

5. **Write the knowledge base:**
   - Save all chunks to `knowledge_base.jsonl`
   - One JSON object per line (JSONL)

6. **Sanity-check before shipping:**
   - Print the total chunk count
   - Manually read **5 random chunks**
   - Confirm they are coherent and not cut mid-sentence
   - Especially exclusion clauses - they must stay intact

7. **Ship to your program repo:**
   - Commit and push `knowledge_base.jsonl` to your program repo root
   - Suggested commit: `git add knowledge_base.jsonl && git commit -m "day 6: chunked knowledge base" && git push`
   - Hit **Verify my repo** below - checks fetch your pushed file

### Submit your answers

Answer these below in order (they prove you actually did the build):

1. What **chunk_size** does this mission's `RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter` use?
2. What **chunk_overlap** does this mission use?
3. What is the **deliverable filename** (JSONL knowledge base at the repo root)?


Objectives:
- Apply recursive character splitting with chunk_size=500 and chunk_overlap=50
- Attach filtering metadata (source_file, source_type, plan_type, section) to every chunk
- Unify Day 4 plan rows and Day 5 policy text into one knowledge_base.jsonl
- Sanity-check chunk coherence (especially exclusion clauses)

Tools:
- langchain-text-splitters
- JSONL
- Python

Videos:
- RAG Tutorial: Text Chunking Strategies for Better RAG Performance

heading: Day 7 (Module 3): Embeddings Explained
text:
Module 3: Embeddings & Vector Search

Brief:
## Mission: Embeddings Explained

Understand how text becomes vectors, and generate embeddings for your coverage knowledge base. Expect about **2–3 hours**.

**Concepts to learn**

- **What embeddings are** - dense vector representations of meaning
- **Popular embedding models** - OpenAI `text-embedding-3`, Sentence-Transformers, Cohere Embed
- **Similarity metrics** - cosine similarity, dot product, Euclidean distance
- **Dimensionality trade-offs** - cost vs performance across embedding models

### Your repo layout (verification checks these exact paths)

```

├── knowledge_base.jsonl          ← from Day 6 (input)

Module 3: Embeddings & Vector Search

Brief:
## Mission: The Retrieval / Matching Engine - Structured + Vector Search

Build the engine that decides, per member question, whether to query SQL (plans/claims), the vector DB (policy wording), or both. Expect about **3 hours**.

**Concepts to learn**

- **Semantic vs keyword vs hybrid search** - dense + sparse retrieval
- **Re-ranking** - improving precision (e.g. Cohere Rerank)
- **Query routing** - classifying **structured lookup** (plan/claim data) vs **knowledge lookup** (coverage wording) vs **both**
- **Context merging** - combining and de-duplicating results before the LLM sees them

### Your repo layout (verification checks these exact paths)

```
your-program-repo/
├── retrieval_engine.py           ← classifier + sql_lookup + vector_lookup + retrieve
├── retrieval_test_results.md     ← 10 test cases with scores
├── coverage.db                     ← from Day 4
├── knowledge_base.jsonl          ← from Day 6
└── vector_db_notes.md            ← from Day 8
```

### Build steps

1. **Write a lightweight question classifier:**
   - Prompt-based function or simple keyword rules
   - Label each question **structured** (e.g. "what's my deductible", "claim status"), **unstructured** (e.g. "is X procedure covered"), or **both**

2. **Implement `sql_lookup(question)`:**
   - Convert structured questions into SQL against your Day 4 plans/claims schema
   - Start with a template, or have the LLM generate SQL

3. **Implement `vector_lookup(question)`:**
   - Embed the question
   - Query your vector DB for the **top-5** relevant policy chunks

4. **Implement `retrieve(question)`:**
   - Route to `sql_lookup`, `vector_lookup`, or both based on the classifier
   - Merge and de-duplicate results into one context block

5. **Build a test harness** with **10 varied questions**, e.g.:
   - "what's my copay"
   - "is maternity care covered on the Bronze plan"
   - "status of claim C-2031"
   - at least one mixed question needing **both** sources

### Build steps

Brief:
## Mission: Fine-Tuning - Concepts & When to Use It

Understand when fine-tuning beats RAG/prompting, and prepare a fine-tuning dataset for consistent coverage-communication tone. Expect about **2.5 hours**.

**Concepts to learn**

- **Fine-tuning vs RAG vs prompting** - decision framework
- **Full fine-tuning vs PEFT** - LoRA / QLoRA
- **When fine-tuning helps a coverage chatbot** - consistent empathetic tone, correct disclaimer usage, domain jargon (deductible, coinsurance, copay) - **not** new factual knowledge about specific plans
- **Dataset prep** - format, size, quality bar

### Your repo layout (verification checks these exact paths)

```
your-program-repo/
├── fine_tune_dataset.jsonl       ← full curated set (20–30 examples)
├── fine_tune_train.jsonl         ← 25 training examples
├── fine_tune_test.jsonl          ← 5 held-out examples (do NOT train on these)
└── fine_tune_prep_notes.md       ← issues FT can vs cannot fix
```

### Build steps

1. **Review Day 10–13 test logs** and identify **3 recurring issues**:
   - Which ones fine-tuning could fix (e.g. forgetting the disclaimer, inconsistent tone)?
   - Which are actually retrieval problems (fine-tuning won't fix those)?

{"messages": [{"role": "system", "content": "..."}, {"role": "user", "content": "..."}, {"role": "assistant", "content": "..."}]}
```

4. **Validate every line:**

5. **Split the data:**
   - Training set: **25** examples → `fine_tune_train.jsonl`

### Build steps

   - **OpenAI:** upload training file via `client.files.create()`, start a job with `client.fine_tuning.jobs.create()`

4. **Run your 5 held-out test questions** from Day 14 through:

## Mission: Conversation Memory & Context Management

Give the chatbot short- and long-term memory across a conversation - including remembering which plan the member is asking about. Expect about **3 hours**.

├── guardrails_config.py          ← input + output guardrails
├── adversarial_tests.md          ← 5 prompts with pass/fail
└── coverage-chatbot-api/main.py  ← /chat logging uses redact_pii
```

Use **synthetic / fake** PHI only - never real member data.

### Build steps

1. **Write `GOVERNANCE.md`** covering:
   - data sources used and their sensitivity
   - PHI/PII fields present (`member_id`, claim details, procedures)
   - bias risks (e.g. plan-tier assumptions)
   - who's accountable for reviewing chatbot outputs

2. **Scan `knowledge_base.jsonl` and SQL tables** for likely PHI/PII columns, then write `redact_pii(text)`:
   - regex, **or**
   - free/open-source Presidio
   - Cover names, member IDs, and other identifiers

3. **Unit test `redact_pii`** with **3** sample strings containing fake PHI/PII, then wire it into your `/chat` endpoint's logging code.

4. **Install Guardrails AI:**
   - `pip install guardrails-ai`
   - Define an **input** guardrail that rejects/flags prompt-injection patterns
   - Examples: "ignore previous instructions", "show me another member's claims"

5. **Define an output guardrail** that:
   - scans for PHI/PII leakage (reuse `redact_pii`)
   - flags anything resembling a medical diagnosis (e.g. "you should take", "your condition is")
   - redirects those to a licensed-provider disclaimer

6. **Write 5 adversarial test prompts** and run them through the full pipeline:
   - a jailbreak attempt
   - a request for another member's claim data
   - a medical-advice question
   - an off-topic question
   - a PHI-fishing question

7. **Log pass/fail** in `adversarial_tests.md` and fix any guardrail that missed:
   - Note in `GOVERNANCE.md` that production use requires a formal compliance review beyond this exercise

8. **Ship to your program repo:**

   - Suggested commit: `git add GOVERNANCE.md redact_pii.py guardrails_config.py adversarial_tests.md && git commit -m "day 25: governance + guardrails" && git push`

- Implement and unit-test redact_pii; wire into /chat logging
- Add input/output guardrails (injection, leakage, medical-advice redirects)

heading: Day 26 (Module 7): Token Governance, Cost Management & Experiment Design
text:
Module 7: Governance & Evaluation

Brief:
## Mission: Token Governance, Cost Management & Experiment Design

Add token/cost logging, rate limiting, response caching, and a designed A/B experiment across two chatbot variants. Expect about **4 hours**.

**Concepts to learn**

- **Token counting** with `tiktoken` on prompts and completions
- **Cost logging** from published per-1K-token rates
- **Rate limiting** per member
- **Exact-match caching** for general questions (never for member-specific ones)
- **Experiment design** - hypothesis, metric, sample size, decision rule

### Your repo layout (verification checks these exact paths)

```
your-program-repo/
├── token_utils.py                ← count_tokens(text)
├── coverage-chatbot-api/
│   └── main.py                   ← /chat logs tokens, rate limit, cache
├── experiment_design.md          ← one-page A/B design
├── ab_test_results.md            ← 15 questions, both variants, scores + conclusion
└── token_usage.csv               ← or SQLite table for usage logs (optional path)
```

### Build steps

1. **Install and count tokens:**
   - `pip install tiktoken`
   - Write `count_tokens(text)` in `token_utils.py`
   - Call it on every prompt + completion inside your `/chat` endpoint

2. **Log usage** for each request to a CSV or SQLite table:
   - `{session_id, timestamp, input_tokens, output_tokens, estimated_cost}`
   - Estimate cost from your provider's published per-1K-token rate

3. **Add a simple rate limiter:**
   - Free `slowapi` library, **or** a manual dict-based counter
   - Cap requests **per member per minute**

4. **Implement an exact-match cache** for repeated **general-coverage** questions:
   - Hash the normalized question
   - Member-specific questions (e.g. claim status) must **never** be cached
   - Test that a repeated general question hits the cache

5. **Write a one-page experiment design** in `experiment_design.md`:
   - Pick two variants (e.g. Day 12 prompt A vs E, or two Day 6 chunk-size settings)
   - Include: hypothesis, metric (e.g. % of answers rated "good"), sample size (**15** questions), decision rule

6. **Build a small test harness** that runs the same **15** coverage/claims questions through both variants and logs both answer sets side by side.

7. **Score and conclude** in `ab_test_results.md`:
   - Manually (or with an LLM-as-judge prompt) score each answer
   - Tabulate results
   - Write which variant wins, by how much, and whether the difference feels meaningful given the small sample size

8. **Ship to your program repo:**
   - Commit helpers, updated `/chat`, and experiment docs
   - Suggested commit: `git add token_utils.py coverage-chatbot-api/main.py experiment_design.md ab_test_results.md && git commit -m "day 26: tokens cost cache AB test" && git push`
   - Hit **Verify my repo** below

### Submit your answers

Answer these below in order (they prove you actually did the build):

1. What is the name of the **token-counting helper function**?
2. How many **questions** are in the A/B experiment sample?
3. What is the **filename** of your one-page experiment design doc?


Objectives:
- Count prompt/completion tokens with tiktoken on every /chat call
- Log session usage and estimated cost; rate-limit per member per minute
- Cache exact-match general questions only (never claim/member-specific)
- Run a 15-question A/B test with design doc, scores, and a clear conclusion

Tools:
- tiktoken
- slowapi
- caching
- A/B testing

heading: Day 27 (Module 7): Evaluation Frameworks
text:
Module 7: Governance & Evaluation

Brief:
## Mission: Evaluation Frameworks

Measure chatbot quality systematically with RAGAS (faithfulness, relevancy, context precision/recall), then improve your weakest metric. Expect about **3 hours**.

**Concepts to learn**

- **RAG evaluation datasets** - question / ideal-answer pairs with retrieved context
- **RAGAS metrics** - faithfulness, answer_relevancy, context_precision, context_recall
- **Iterate from the scorecard** - weakest metric → one concrete fix → re-eval

### Your repo layout (verification checks these exact paths)

```
your-program-repo/
├── ragas_eval_set.jsonl          ← 15–20 question / ideal-answer pairs (CSV ok too)
├── ragas_run.py                  ← run pipeline + RAGAS evaluate()
├── ragas_scorecard.md            ← scores, weakest metric, hypothesis, re-run delta
└── rag_chatbot.py / retrieval    ← full RAG pipeline under test
```

If you prefer CSV, also keep a JSONL export or name the CSV `ragas_eval_set.csv` and reference it in the scorecard.

### Build steps

1. **Install RAGAS:**
   - `pip install ragas datasets`

2. **Build a test set of 15–20** question / ideal-answer pairs covering:
   - deductibles
   - exclusions
   - claims status
   - plan comparisons
   - Save as `ragas_eval_set.jsonl` (or CSV)

3. **Run each question through your full RAG pipeline**, capturing:
   - question
   - retrieved contexts
   - generated answer
   - ground-truth (ideal) answer

4. **Format a RAGAS-compatible dataset** and run `evaluate()` with:
   - `faithfulness`
   - `answer_relevancy`
   - `context_precision`
   - `context_recall`

5. **Review the scorecard** in `ragas_scorecard.md`:
   - Identify your **weakest metric** (often `context_recall` on exclusion clauses)
   - Hypothesize why (e.g. chunk size too large, embedding model too weak)

6. **Make one concrete change** based on the finding (e.g. reduce chunk size for exclusion sections) and **re-run** the eval to see if the score improves. Log before/after in the scorecard.

7. **Ship to your program repo:**
   - Commit the eval set, runner, and scorecard
   - Suggested commit: `git add ragas_eval_set.jsonl ragas_run.py ragas_scorecard.md && git commit -m "day 27: RAGAS scorecard + one fix" && git push`
   - Hit **Verify my repo** below

### Submit your answers

Answer these below in order (they prove you actually did the build):

1. Which Python package (with `datasets`) do you install for this eval?
2. About how many **question / ideal-answer pairs** are in the test set (minimum)?
3. What is the **filename** of your written scorecard (weakest metric + re-run)?


Objectives:
- Build a 15–20 pair coverage eval set (deductibles, exclusions, claims, plan comparisons)
- Run the full RAG pipeline and evaluate with RAGAS faithfulness/relevancy/precision/recall
- Identify the weakest metric and hypothesize why
- Make one concrete fix and re-run to measure improvement

Tools:
- ragas
- datasets
- RAG evaluation

Videos:
- RAGAS: How to Evaluate a RAG Application Like a Pro for Beginners

heading: Day 28 (Module 8): Docker - Containerizing the Coverage Chatbot
text:
Module 8: Containerization, Kubernetes & Production

Brief:
## Mission: Docker - Containerizing the Coverage Chatbot

Package backend and frontend into containers with multi-stage builds, docker-compose, and health checks. Expect about **3 hours**.

**Concepts to learn**

- **Multi-stage Dockerfiles** - builder installs deps; final stage stays slim
- **docker-compose** - backend + frontend + volumes + `env_file`
- **Container health checks** - `HEALTHCHECK` + `/health`

├── Dockerfile.frontend           ← Streamlit frontend (if separate)
├── docker-compose.yml            ← wires services + Chroma volume + env_file
├── .env.example                  ← keys as placeholders only (never commit real secrets)
├── .dockerignore
└── docker_notes.md               ← confirm compose up + healthy status
```

If your backend Dockerfile lives at `coverage-chatbot-api/Dockerfile`, keep `docker-compose.yml` at the repo root and point `build:` at that path. Never hardcode API keys.

### Build steps

5. **Build and run locally:**

6. **Add a `HEALTHCHECK`** instruction to the backend Dockerfile and confirm `docker ps` shows it as **healthy**. Log proof in `docker_notes.md`.

7. **Ship to your program repo:**

2. Which Dockerfile instruction defines the container health probe?
3. How should API keys be passed into compose (not hardcoded)?

heading: Day 29 (Module 8): Kubernetes - Orchestrating & Scaling the Deployment
text:
Module 8: Containerization, Kubernetes & Production

Brief:
## Mission: Kubernetes - Orchestrating & Scaling the Deployment

Deploy the chatbot to a local Minikube cluster with Deployments, Services, Secrets, probes, scaling, and rolling updates. Expect about **3.5 hours**.

**Concepts to learn**

- **Minikube + kubectl** local cluster workflow
- **Deployments & Services** - replicas, ClusterIP / NodePort
- **Secrets** via `envFrom` (never plain YAML in git)
- **readinessProbe / livenessProbe**, scale, and rolling updates

### Your repo layout (verification checks these exact paths)

```
your-program-repo/
├── k8s/
│   ├── backend-deployment.yaml
│   ├── backend-service.yaml
│   ├── frontend-deployment.yaml
│   └── frontend-service.yaml
├── k8s_notes.md                  ← scale + rolling update + teardown notes
└── docker-compose.yml            ← from Day 28
```

Create Secrets with `kubectl create secret` - do **not** commit real API keys in YAML.

### Build steps

1. **Install Minikube and kubectl**, then start a local cluster:
   - `minikube start`

2. **Get Day 28 images into Minikube:**
   - Push to a registry Minikube can reach, **or**
   - `minikube image load` your local images

3. **Write manifests** under `k8s/`:
   - `backend-deployment.yaml` (**2** replicas)
   - `backend-service.yaml` (ClusterIP or NodePort)
   - Same pair for the frontend

4. **Store the LLM API key as a Kubernetes Secret:**
   - `kubectl create secret ...`
   - Reference it via `envFrom` in the deployment spec
   - Never commit the secret value in plain YAML

5. **Add probes and apply:**
   - `readinessProbe` and `livenessProbe` pointing at `/health`
   - `kubectl apply -f` the manifests
   - Confirm pods reach **Running / Ready**

6. **Test scale and rolling update**, then tear down:
   - `kubectl scale deployment backend --replicas=3`
   - Change the image tag and `kubectl apply` again - confirm zero-downtime rollout
   - `kubectl delete` to tear down
   - Log what you observed in `k8s_notes.md`

7. **Ship to your program repo:**
   - Commit manifests + notes (no secret values)
   - Suggested commit: `git add k8s/ k8s_notes.md && git commit -m "day 29: minikube deploy scale rollout" && git push`
   - Hit **Verify my repo** below

### Submit your answers

Answer these below in order (they prove you actually did the build):

1. What command starts the local Minikube cluster?
2. How many **replicas** does the initial backend Deployment use?
3. Which probe types do you point at `/health` (readiness + liveness)?


Objectives:
- Start Minikube and load Day 28 images into the cluster
- Write backend/frontend Deployment + Service manifests (2 backend replicas)
- Inject the LLM key via Secret + envFrom; add /health probes
- Practice scale to 3, rolling update, then tear down with notes

Tools:
- Kubernetes
- Minikube
- kubectl

Videos:
- Deploy Node.js With Docker and Kubernetes Tutorial for Beginners
- Minikube Basics and How to Get Started with Kubernetes

heading: Day 30 (Module 8): Monitoring & Observability
text:
Module 8: Containerization, Kubernetes & Production

Brief:
## Mission: Monitoring & Observability

Wire Langfuse tracing into the deployed chatbot and practice debugging pods with kubectl. Expect about **2.5 hours**.

**Concepts to learn**

- **LLM observability** - latency, tokens, full prompt/response traces
- **kubectl debugging** - `logs -f` and `describe pod`
- **Production alert sketch** - error rate, p95 latency, daily cost ceiling

### Your repo layout (verification checks these exact paths)

```
your-program-repo/
├── coverage-chatbot-api/
│   └── main.py                   ← Langfuse tracing on LLM calls
├── observability_notes.md        ← Langfuse confirm + kubectl debug + alert sketch
└── k8s/                          ← Day 29 manifests (redeploy with tracing)
```

Store Langfuse keys in Secrets / `env_file` - never commit them.

### Build steps

1. **Sign up for Langfuse** (free cloud or self-host) and install:
   - `pip install langfuse`

2. **Wrap your LLM calls** with Langfuse's tracing decorator / context manager so every request logs:
   - latency
   - token usage
   - full prompt / response

3. **Redeploy to your Day 29 Minikube cluster** and generate a handful of test conversations:
   - Open the Langfuse dashboard
   - Confirm traces are appearing
   - Note confirmation in `observability_notes.md`

4. **Practice kubectl debugging** on a deliberately broken pod (e.g. a bad env var):
   - `kubectl logs -f <pod-name>`
   - `kubectl describe pod <pod-name>`
   - Document what you saw

5. **Sketch production alerts** (paper or in the notes doc):
   - error-rate threshold
   - p95 latency threshold
   - daily cost ceiling

6. **Push the final code** (with tracing wired in) to GitHub.

7. **Ship notes + traced code:**
   - Suggested commit: `git add coverage-chatbot-api/main.py observability_notes.md && git commit -m "day 30: langfuse tracing + ops notes" && git push`
   - Hit **Verify my repo** below

### Submit your answers

Answer these below in order (they prove you actually did the build):

1. Which `pip` package installs Langfuse?
2. Which kubectl command follows live logs for a pod (`kubectl logs …`)?
3. What is the **filename** of your observability / alerts notes?


Objectives:
- Install Langfuse and wrap LLM calls with tracing (latency, tokens, prompt/response)
- Redeploy to Minikube and confirm traces in the Langfuse dashboard
- Practice kubectl logs -f and describe on a broken pod
- Sketch production alerts: error rate, p95 latency, daily cost ceiling

heading: Day 31 (Module 8): Capstone - End-to-End Review & Roadmap
text:
Module 8: Containerization, Kubernetes & Production

Brief:
## Mission: Capstone - End-to-End Review & Roadmap

Do a full live walkthrough of your Kubernetes-deployed chatbot, capture observability evidence, write a retrospective + v2 roadmap, record a short demo, and archive a clean GitHub repo. Expect about **3 hours**.

**Concepts to learn**

- **End-to-end acceptance** across structured, policy, claims, multi-turn, and adversarial paths
- **Portfolio packaging** - demo video, README, retrospective, roadmap
- **Responsible next steps** - formal compliance/legal review before real member data

### Your repo layout (verification checks these exact paths)

```
your-program-repo/
├── README.md                     ← clean summary of what you built
├── capstone_walkthrough.md       ← 5 scenario results + Langfuse evidence note
├── retrospective.md              ← what worked / hard / do differently
├── v2_roadmap.md                 ← prioritized next features + compliance note
└── (optional) demo link in README
```

You do not need to commit the demo video binary - link it from README (Drive/YouTube/unlisted).

### Build steps

1. **Full live walkthrough** of your Kubernetes-deployed chatbot - confirm each path is handled as designed:
   - a structured coverage question
   - a policy-wording question
   - a claim-status lookup
   - a multi-turn follow-up
   - one adversarial / off-topic question
   - Log results in `capstone_walkthrough.md`

2. **Check Langfuse** for the session and screenshot the trace as evidence of end-to-end observability (note/link the screenshot in the walkthrough doc).

3. **Write a 1-page retrospective** in `retrospective.md`:
   - what worked well
   - what was harder than expected
   - 2–3 things you'd do differently starting over

4. **Write a prioritized v2 roadmap** in `v2_roadmap.md`, e.g.:
   - multi-modal (image) support for scanned documents
   - voice input/output
   - additional languages
   - scaling to a managed cloud Kubernetes service
   - **critically** - a formal compliance/legal review before touching any real member data

5. **Record a 2–3 minute demo video** (OS built-in screen recorder) walking through the chatbot for your portfolio. Link it from `README.md`.

6. **Archive the whole project** in GitHub with a clean `README.md` summarizing what you built (code, docs, this program).

7. **Ship the capstone docs:**
   - Suggested commit: `git add README.md capstone_walkthrough.md retrospective.md v2_roadmap.md && git commit -m "day 31: capstone demo docs + roadmap" && git push`
   - Hit **Verify my repo** below

### Submit your answers

Answer these below in order (they prove you actually did the build):

1. How many **live walkthrough scenarios** do you run (coverage, policy, claim, multi-turn, adversarial)?
2. About how long should the portfolio **demo video** be (minutes)?
3. What is the **filename** of your prioritized v2 roadmap?


Objectives:
- Run five live scenarios on the K8s-deployed chatbot and log results
- Capture Langfuse trace evidence for the session
- Write a retrospective and a prioritized v2 roadmap (incl. compliance review)

heading: Day 3 (AI): Text is Data - Turning Words into Numbers
text:
**Context:** Machines don't read words. They read numbers. Preprocessing is the first transformation that turns raw human language into something a model can learn from.

**Real-World Impact:** Every NLP system - search, chatbots, classification - starts with tokenization and preprocessing. Get this wrong and the rest of the pipeline collapses.

**What to do:**
- Tokenize a paragraph using NLTK or spaCy
- Remove stop words and punctuation from a sample text
- Convert tokens to a simple bag-of-words representation

heading: Day 4 (AI): Vectors - Teaching Meaning to Machines
text:
**Context:** Bag-of-words counts words. Vectors capture meaning. When you embed a sentence, similar concepts end up close together in vector space - that's what lets AI "understand."

**Real-World Impact:** Embeddings power semantic search, recommendation systems, RAG, and clustering. They are the foundation of modern AI retrieval.

**What to do:**
- Install and import `sentence-transformers` in Colab
- Generate embeddings for 5 sentences (mix of similar and different meanings)
- Compare two sentences for similarity using cosine distance
- Observe which pairs score highest - does it match your intuition?

**Submission:**
- A similarity score between sentence pairs
- Short reflection on what surprised you

Objectives:
- Generate sentence embeddings
- Measure semantic similarity with cosine distance
- Develop intuition for vector space

heading: Day 5 (AI): Build a Mini Search Engine

heading: Day 6 (AI): What is Machine Learning? Build an Intuition

heading: Day 8 (AI): How Machines Read Human Language
text:

heading: Day 9 (AI): Teaching AI Semantic Meaning Through Vectors
text:
**Focus Area:** Vector Representation and Cosine Similarity
Humans understand that 'king' and 'queen' are related, but computers only understand numbers. AI systems convert words and sentences into numerical vectors to compare meaning mathematically. Build a semantic similarity workflow using TF-IDF vectorisation and cosine similarity to quantify how related different pieces of text are.

**Tools:** Python, scikit-learn, NumPy, matplotlib

**What to do:**
- Write a short explanation of why plain text cannot be compared directly and why numerical vector representation is necessary for machine processing
- Convert a set of 10 sentences covering three distinct topics into TF-IDF vector representations using scikit-learn's TfidfVectorizer
- Calculate pairwise cosine similarity scores between all sentence combinations and store the results in a NumPy matrix
- Build a find_similar(query, corpus, top_k) function that accepts a new sentence and returns the most similar corpus sentences with their scores
- Test the function with semantically similar pairs such as 'dog' vs 'puppy' and dissimilar pairs such as 'dog' vs 'airplane' and print all scores
- Visualise the 10x10 similarity matrix as a heatmap using matplotlib with labelled axes so the clustering pattern is visible
- Document in writing why cosine similarity measures the angle between vectors rather than the distance, and why that distinction matters for text comparison

**Submission:**
- Semantic similarity demo notebook with heatmap visualisation, find_similar() function output for multiple test pairs, and written explanation of the vector math behind cosine similarity

Objectives:
- Write a short explanation of why plain text cannot be compared directly and why numerical vector representation is necessary for machine processing
- Convert a set of 10 sentences covering three distinct topics into TF-IDF vector representations using scikit-learn's TfidfVectorizer
- Calculate pairwise cosine similarity scores between all sentence combinations and store the results in a NumPy matrix
- Build a find_similar(query, corpus, top_k) function that accepts a new sentence and returns the most similar corpus sentences with their scores

heading: Day 11 (AI): Build Your First Document Retrieval System
text:
**Focus Area:** Information Retrieval
Modern AI systems do not generate answers from nothing - they first retrieve relevant information. Build a mini retrieval engine that accepts user queries and returns the most relevant documents from a knowledge base, ranked by similarity score, with a threshold below which it honestly admits it cannot find anything useful.

**What to do:**

heading: Day 12 (AI): Chunking Strategies for Long Document Processing
text:
**Focus Area:** Context Chunking
Real documents - research papers, manuals, articles - are too long to fit into LLM context windows. Chunking splits large documents into smaller overlapping pieces without losing meaning at the boundaries. Build a chunking experiment comparing multiple strategies on the same document to understand how chunk design affects retrieval quality.

**Tools:** Python, LangChain

**What to do:**

- Compare the retrieved chunks across all configurations for the same query and print which configuration returns the most contextually complete result

- Implement recursive character text splitting using LangChain's RecursiveCharacterTextSplitter with configurable chunk_size and chunk_overlap parameters

heading: Day 13 (AI): Understanding Embeddings as Semantic Coordinates
text:
**Focus Area:** Dense Embeddings
TF-IDF vectors fail when words are different but meanings are the same. Embeddings solve this by encoding semantic meaning as dense numerical coordinates in high-dimensional space. heading: Day 14 (AI): Build a Semantic Search Engine
text:

heading: Day 15 (AI): Build Your First RAG Pipeline
text:

LLMs hallucinate because they generate from training data alone. RAG systems fix this by retrieving relevant documents first and injecting them into the prompt as grounding context. - Draw a complete RAG system architecture diagram showing every step from user query to final response with each transformation labelled

heading: Day 18 (AI): Why LLMs Hallucinate and How to Measure It
text:
**Focus Area:** Hallucination Understanding and Detection
Hallucination is not a random bug - it is a predictable consequence of how language models generate text by predicting the next most likely token rather than retrieving verified facts. Understanding the mechanics of hallucination is essential before you can systematically reduce it. Build a hallucination measurement experiment that quantifies how often and why your LLM fabricates information.

**Tools:** Python, OpenAI API

**What to do:**
- Create a dataset of 20 factual questions where you know the ground-truth correct answers - cover at least three different knowledge domains to test breadth
- Run each question through GPT-4o-mini with no context and no retrieval, recording every response verbatim in a structured results dictionary
- Manually evaluate each response and classify it as correct, partially correct, or hallucinated using explicit criteria you define before scoring begins
- Categorise hallucinated responses by type: fabricated specific facts, outdated information presented as current, confident wrong answer, or plausible-sounding but unverifiable claim
- Run the same 20 questions through your Day 15 RAG pipeline and record all responses in the same structured format
- Calculate a hallucination rate percentage for both conditions - no context and with RAG - and compare the two numbers
- Build a multi-signal hallucination detector in Python with four independent checks: (1) unsupported claim detection - flag any specific numerical claim, named entity, or date in the response that does not appear in the retrieved context; (2) retrieval overlap check - compute token-level overlap between the response and the retrieved chunks using Jaccard similarity and flag responses below 0.15 overlap; (3) contradiction detection - send a secondary LLM call asking 'Does this response contradict the provided context? Answer yes or no.' and flag positives; (4) citation absence check - flag any response that makes verifiable factual assertions but contains no reference to a source document or passage. Combine all four signals into a final confidence score and print a per-response breakdown

**Submission:**
- Hallucination measurement report with 20-question test dataset, categorised failure table, hallucination rate comparison between no-context and RAG conditions, and four-signal rule-based detection script with per-response breakdown output

Objectives:
- Create a dataset of 20 factual questions where you know the ground-truth correct answers - cover at least three different knowledge domains to test breadth
- Run each question through GPT-4o-mini with no context and no retrieval, recording every response verbatim in a structured results dictionary
- Manually evaluate each response and classify it as correct, partially correct, or hallucinated using explicit criteria you define before scoring begins
- Categorise hallucinated responses by type: fabricated specific facts, outdated information presented as current, confident wrong answer, or plausible-sounding but unverifiable claim
- Run the same 20 questions through your Day 15 RAG pipeline and record all responses in the same structured format
- Calculate a hallucination rate percentage for both conditions - no context and with RAG - and compare the two numbers

- Build a prompt version dictionary that stores each version as a key with its average eval score and a one-line description of what changed relative to the previous version
- Identify which single technique produced the largest improvement for your specific task and write a hypothesis explaining why it worked better than the others
- Design a grounding system prompt for your RAG assistant that explicitly instructs the model to refuse answering anything not directly supported by the provided context
- Test the grounding prompt against five out-of-context questions and print whether the model refused correctly or answered from training data anyway in each case

**Submission:**

heading: Day 21 (AI): What Makes AI Products Actually Good
text:
**Focus Area:** AI Product Quality Thinking
Most AI demos look impressive but fall apart in real use. The gap between a working prototype and a genuinely good AI product is product thinking - understanding what real users need, where systems break under realistic inputs, and what quality means beyond accuracy on your own test cases. heading: Day 22 (AI): Designing Production-Ready AI APIs
text:
**Focus Area:** API Design for AI Systems
AI APIs face unique design challenges that standard REST APIs do not: streaming responses, token limits, retry logic for flaky LLM calls, and expensive operations that must be short-circuited before invalid inputs reach the model. Design and build a production-grade AI API with proper validation, error handling, streaming, and structured error codes.

**Tools:** Python, FastAPI, Pydantic

**What to do:**
- Redesign your Day 20 FastAPI endpoint using Pydantic request and response models with typed fields, field validators, and example values in the schema
- Add input validation that rejects queries under five characters, over 1000 characters, or containing only whitespace or special characters - each returning a descriptive error message with an error code
- Implement retry logic with exponential backoff for OpenAI API rate limit errors using a try-except loop with configurable sleep intervals and a maximum retry count
- Add streaming response support using FastAPI's StreamingResponse so the first tokens appear in the client before the full generation is complete
- Implement a 15-second request timeout: if the full pipeline does not complete in time, return a structured partial response with a LLM_TIMEOUT error code rather than hanging indefinitely
- Define three structured error codes with consistent JSON shapes: RETRIEVAL_FAILURE, LLM_TIMEOUT, and INPUT_INVALID - each including code, message, and request_id fields
- Deliberately trigger each error path and print the response body to verify every error case returns the correct structured response and the right HTTP status code

**Submission:**
- Production-grade FastAPI AI endpoint with Pydantic models, streaming responses, retry logic with exponential backoff, timeout handling, and verified test output for all three error codes

heading: Day 24 (AI): Building Conversation Memory Systems
text:
**Focus Area:** Stateful AI Conversations
LLMs are stateless - each API call forgets the previous one entirely. Real assistant products require conversation memory so follow-up questions like 'what did you mean by that?' work correctly without the user repeating context. Build a memory system that maintains conversation state across multiple turns without overflowing the token limit.

**Tools:** Python, LangChain, OpenAI API, FastAPI

**What to do:**
- Implement a ConversationHistory class that stores message history per session as a list of role-content pairs and exposes append(), get_context(), and clear() methods
- Modify your FastAPI endpoint to accept an optional session_id parameter and maintain a separate ConversationHistory instance per session in a server-side dictionary
- Build a context injection strategy that includes only the last five turns of conversation history in each prompt to avoid exceeding the model's token limit
- Test multi-turn conversations by sending a sequence of five messages where turns three and five use pronouns that only make sense with memory of the earlier turns
- Implement memory window truncation: when a session exceeds 10 turns, summarise the oldest five turns into a single context block using an LLM call and replace them with that summary
- Run the same five-turn conversation with and without memory active and compare the quality of the follow-up answers
- Quantify the memory trade-off: calculate the additional token cost per turn at your current window size and estimate the monthly cost difference at 1000 daily users averaging 10 turns per session

**Submission:**
- Session-aware AI assistant with ConversationHistory class, memory window truncation, five-turn conversation test outputs with and without memory, and a written token cost analysis

text:

After two weeks of building, your AI system is functional but probably structurally messy. Hardcoded values, duplicated logic, and missing tests accumulate quietly and slow down every future day. heading: Day 26 (AI): Introduction to AI Agents and the ReAct Pattern
text:
**Focus Area:** AI Agents
A standard LLM answers a question in one step. An AI agent plans, uses tools, observes results, and decides what to do next autonomously. Understand agent architecture from the inside by building a ReAct-pattern agent manually - without a framework - so you can see exactly how reasoning and acting combine and precisely where autonomous decision-making breaks down.

**Tools:** Python, OpenAI API

**What to do:**
- Study the ReAct pattern and implement the full loop manually in Python: the LLM produces a Thought, names an Action with parameters, you execute the action, feed the Observation back into the next prompt, and repeat until the LLM outputs a Final Answer
- Implement three tool functions: a calculator(expression) that evaluates arithmetic, a search_docs(query) that retrieves from your Day 11 knowledge base, and a get_today() that returns the current date as a string
- Write a tool_registry dictionary mapping tool names to functions and build a dispatch function that parses the LLM's named action and routes it to the correct tool
- Run the agent on five multi-step problems that require using more than one tool in sequence - for example, a question that needs a document lookup followed by a calculation on the retrieved value
- Print the full Thought → Action → Observation trace for every step of every problem so the entire reasoning chain is visible and inspectable
- Identify and document where the agent goes wrong: looping without progress, hallucinating a tool output it never actually received, or selecting the wrong tool for the task
- Write a short analysis of what makes an agent reliable versus unpredictable, grounded specifically in the failure patterns you observed during your five test problems

**Submission:**
- Manual ReAct agent with three tools and a dispatch function, full reasoning traces for all five test problems, documented failure patterns, and written reliability analysis

text:

Day 26's manual ReAct agent parsed tool calls from raw LLM text output - fragile and error-prone when the model formats its output slightly differently. heading: Day 28 (AI): Multi-Step AI Workflows with State Management
text:
**Focus Area:** Stateful Multi-Step Agent Workflows
Real-world AI tasks rarely finish in a single step. Generating a research report requires searching, extracting key points, synthesising findings, and formatting output - four sequential steps where each depends on the output of the last. Build a multi-step workflow with persistent state so a partially completed run can resume from the last checkpoint rather than restarting from scratch.

**Tools:** Python, LangChain, OpenAI API

**What to do:**
- Design a four-step research workflow and implement each step as a standalone Python function: search_sources(topic), extract_key_points(chunks), synthesise_findings(points), and format_report(synthesis)
- Build a WorkflowState dataclass that carries the topic, retrieved chunks, extracted points, synthesis text, and final report as fields - passed between every step
- Wire the four step functions together in a run_workflow(topic) orchestrator that passes the updated state through each step sequentially
- Implement checkpoint saving: after each step completes, serialise the WorkflowState to a JSON file on disk named after the step so a crashed run can restart from the last saved point
- Test resume functionality by intentionally raising an exception during step three, then modify the orchestrator to detect the checkpoint file and skip already-completed steps on restart
- Add step-level error handling: if any step raises an exception, log the error with the step name and the current state snapshot, then exit cleanly with a partial results file
- Run the complete workflow on three different research topics and compare the structure and quality of the three generated reports

**Submission:**
- Multi-step research workflow with WorkflowState dataclass, checkpoint saving and tested resume, step-level error handling, and three generated research reports from different topics

heading: Day 29 (AI): Building AI Evaluation Systems
text:
**Focus Area:** AI Evaluation and Measurement
You cannot improve what you cannot measure. Automated evaluation systems that objectively score your AI system's outputs are a core production engineering skill - they are what separate teams that iterate based on data from teams that iterate based on gut feel. Build an LLM-as-judge evaluation framework that scores your assistant's answers and runs automatically as a regression test before any deployment.

**Tools:** Python, OpenAI API

**What to do:**

- Build an llm_judge(question, context, answer, ground_truth) function that sends a structured scoring prompt to GPT-4o-mini and returns scores from 1 to 5 for each dimension as a parsed JSON object
- Create a labelled evaluation dataset of 20 question-answer pairs for your Day 20 knowledge assistant where you have written the correct ground-truth answer for each question manually
- Run your assistant on all 20 questions and pass each response through llm_judge(), collecting all scores in a results dictionary
- Calculate aggregate scores per dimension - average groundedness, average correctness, average completeness - and identify which dimension is lowest and by how much
- Build a regression_test_runner() function that runs the full 20-question suite, compares each dimension score against a stored baseline, and prints PASS or FAIL with the specific dimension and score drop if any threshold is breached
- Document the limitations of LLM-as-judge evaluation honestly: where the judge can be wrong, which answer types it cannot score reliably, and when human evaluation is still necessary

**Submission:**
- Automated evaluation framework with llm_judge() function, 20-question labelled dataset, aggregate score report per dimension, regression_test_runner(), and evaluation limitations document
